intuition: Move one pointer one link at a time and another pointer two links at a time. If the list ends, there is no cycle. If it loops, the faster pointer eventually catches the slower one. Compare the actual nodes, because equal stored values do not mean the pointers have met.

Move slow one link and fast two links each iteration. If the list ends, fast reaches an absent node or absent next link and the search terminates. If a cycle exists, both pointers eventually enter it and keep moving around the same finite ring.

Inside a cycle of length c, fast gains one position on slow per iteration. Their relative offset modulo c must eventually reach zero, so they meet at the same object. Compare after moving rather than at initialization, since both pointers initially reference head even in a perfectly ordinary acyclic list.

steps: In [3,2,0,-4] with pos=1, the tail node -4 links back to the node whose value is 2.
Both pointers start at node 3. After the first move, slow is at 2 and fast is at 0.
After the second move, slow is at 0. Fast travels 0→-4→2, so the pointers remain distinct.
After the third move, slow reaches -4. Fast travels 2→0→-4 and reaches that same node object.
The identity comparison succeeds, proving a revisit in the structure. Return true; matching numeric values alone would not have been enough.

codeNotes.code: while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
codeNotes.note: Both guards are needed before the two-link advance. Reaching either missing link proves the forward chain terminates instead of cycling.
The extra step changes the relative offset by one per iteration inside a cycle, guaranteeing a meeting regardless of its length.
Object identity tests whether the pointers occupy the same actual node. Equal values in separate acyclic nodes must not trigger success.

approach: Move one bookmark by one link and the other by two.
Return no if the faster bookmark reaches an end.
Return yes when both bookmarks refer to the same node after moving.
concept.correctness: Without a cycle, advancing along next links eventually ends, so the fast walker cannot keep going or meet the slow walker after moving. In a cycle, both eventually enter it. The fast walker advances one extra link relative to the slow walker each round; modulo the cycle length, it visits every possible separation and reaches zero. Their meeting therefore detects exactly a cycle.

complexity.explanation: The walkers traverse a linear number of links before ending or meeting. Two bookmarks use constant extra memory.

pitfalls: Check the fast walker can take both links.
Do not treat their shared initial position as a detected cycle.
